entries.title: After Mayor Johnson’s CFO jumps ship, aldermanic opponents want outside audit of city's financial statements
entries.summary: <p>Leaders of a renegade City Council coalition are following through on their threat to authorize an outside audit of the city’s finances to reassure Wall Street rating agencies after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/13/ashlee-gabrysch-chief-financial-officer-resigns-chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson" >stunning resignation </a>of Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch. </p><p>The ordinance would authorize Finance Committee Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) to select and engage one or more independent professional services firms to conduct an “impartial and comprehensive review” to determine whether any “material or intentional misstatements of the city’s financial condition” have been made to investors, City Council and the public in any “document, presentation, offering or financial reporting within the last three years.”</p><p>City officials and employees would be compelled to cooperate with the three-year investigation and provide access to all city records, reports and information requested by the designated firms, the ordinance states. Anyone who refuses to cooperate would face “employment sanctions, including suspension or discharge.”</p><p>“In the wake of last week's resignation of the city’s third CFO in a year, we find ourselves at a moment where every effort must be made to secure the public’s confidence in our city’s finances,” Dowell said in a statement about the ordinance she championed with 11 colleagues.</p><p></p><p>A former analyst for Fitch Ratings, Gabrysch resigned Friday after just three months on the job. She is the third person to have served as Mayor Brandon Johnson’s chief financial officer in the last year.</p><p>She quit after being admonished, frozen out and, as sources closes to her said, bullied for publicly and privately contradicting the mayor’s claim that his $17.6 billion budget was 76% structurally balanced.</p><p>Gabrysch said only 56% of the moves the mayor had made to erase a $882 million shortfall were structural, because settlements tied to allegations of police abuse — and the $480 million in borrowing that Johnson ordered to cover those costs — should not count as structural solutions.</p><p>Contacted Monday, Gabrysch welcomed the outside audit, even though it’s likely to take months and Wall Street rating agencies pay more attention to the city’s annual audit.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-990000" name="image-990000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ashlee Gabrysch</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>City of Chicago via LinkedIn</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Chicago has a history of making things look a lot better than they are… We come out with these billion dollar deficits and, somehow, we make them disappear. Residents don’t take it seriously because it really just seems kind of performative rather than actual budgetary strife,” Gabrysch said Monday.</p><p>“If this makes it easier for residents to see that Chicago actually is in a fairly dire fiscal situation where hard decisions… and shared sacrifices have to be made, that can be helpful… Shining some light on the city’s finances — whether or not they discover wrongdoing, but rather showing the nuances of how dire some things have become — could be worthwhile.”</p><p>Gabrysch said she has hired an attorney to determine whether to file a defamation lawsuit against the city for what she called the Johnson administration’s "attempt to smear me and a pretty pathetic attempt at that." </p><p>The mayor's office statement accused Gabrysch of being “largely absent during critical periods of the budget preparation process.” Johnson also asked Inspector General David Glockner to conduct an internal investigation of Gabrysch’s decision to direct the city treasurer to forward a $75 million up-front payment from the New York investment firm that acquired Chicago parking meters “without proper legal authority or following the required processes.”</p><p>Gabrysch said the only meetings she missed during the budget preparation process were to attend conferences that were approved by Chief of Staff Cristina Pacione-Zayas.</p><p>The $75 million payment from Stonepeak Partners was forwarded to the pension funds, only after a veto-proof majority of the City Council authorized it, the mayor signed the ordinance and top mayoral aides were informed that the payment was being made.</p><p>"I'm not a litigious person, [but] it was very hurtful when that came out. I understand what they were trying to do. But I do think that once the letters are [made public] I will be vindicated. The letters will show that this was not done behind anyone's back," she said.</p><p>"Twenty-plus people knew this was happening. If there was a true concern about this money being directed, 20 different people could have raised this issue before the money was released. We also had the ability to withhold money from the pension funds if in some crazy universe the 44 people who had voted for it ultimately changed their minds." </p><p>Gabrysch said she stands by the decisions she made during her three months on the job even though the last stand that she took prompted top mayoral aides to bully her and freeze her out.</p><p>"The city of Chicago’s CFO needs to be able to speak truthfully to residents, to rating agencies, to the City Council... There should be no political spin of that whatsoever," she said. </p><p>“I am not one that is easily bullied. I was certainly told what I could and could not say… When I testified in front of City Council, I said a number of things I was told I could not say. They were not happy with me. I was supposed to report to the mayor and I never met with the mayor one on one ever… I certainly was frozen out from different meetings. They went around me. They pulled me from press conferences that I was initially invited to. They went to my staff rather than me on things that should have gone through me."</p><p>The mayor’s office said it “welcomes any independent audit conducted in accordance with municipal finance standards."</p><p>A consortium of accounting firms approved by the Finance Committee already conducts a Comprehensive Annual Financial Report where the city has “consistently received strong marks for the accuracy and completeness of its financial reporting,” the mayor’s office statement said.</p><p>Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson said there is "nothing that indicates that there are actual fluffing of numbers anywhere." But an outside audit is still worthwhile and it could easily be done by Glockner, former regional chief of enforcement for the Securities Exchange Commission.</p><p></p><p>"There is no trust right now in the administration with the City Council and probably with the markets, so some form of neutral party examination should be done," Ferguson said. "But that is, at best, a months-long project and we have seven weeks to land a balanced budget. As long as it's not a distraction, fine. But nobody should expect any miracles from this alone."</p><p>The first sign of fallout from the Gabrych resignation happened at Monday's Finance Committee meeting.</p><p>A proposed $500 million bond issue to bankroll sewer projects across the city was pulled from the agenda at the Johnson administration's request. That prevented Acting Chief Financial Officer Michael Belsky from having to testify and, potentially being asked about the Gabrysch resignation.</p>

entries.title: Bears report: CB Kyler Gordon out for Monday practice; WR Luther Burden, RB Kyle Monangai active
entries.summary: <p>What happened Monday at Halas Hall:</p><h3><b>Gordon absent</b></h3><h3></h3><p>It’s always a story when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon is out, as he was Monday, though it’s too early to fret about his availability against the Saints on Sunday. Gordon injured his left arm in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/08/bears-buccaneers-inactives-bears-rb-kyle-monangai-remains-out-with-toe-injury" >the Nov. 8 win over the Buccaneers</a> and went to the locker room, but returned to play in that game.</p><p>Gordon missed 14 games last season and the first five of this one, and his ability to stay healthy is crucial to his standing with the team.</p><h3><b>Burden practices</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Bears wide receiver Luther Burden took a brutal helmet-to-helmet hit from Bucs linebacker Reuben Bain, and coach Ben Johnson said he had a concussion. He was back at practice, though, which is promising for Sunday.</p><h3><b>Monangai on track</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Bears haven’t had No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai since his monster game against the Jets on Oct. 4, but the fact that he was questionable on the injury report for the Bucs game signaled he’d be likely to return against the Saints. He practiced Monday.</p><h3><b>Stevenson persists</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Bears cornerback Tyrique Stevenson seems to have a new injury every week, but has been active for all but one game. There was concern that his thumb injury had worsened, but he practiced Monday.</p><h3><b>New face</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Bears have never faced Saints quarterback Tyler Shough. He’s 16th in the NFL with a 90.2 passer rating, but is coming off a dismal performance: 187 yards, a touchdown, an interception and a fumble.</p>

entries.title: Cook County Jail wrongful death lawsuit set to settle for record $7.25 million
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was produced by </i><a class="Link" href="http://injusticewatch.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Injustice Watch</i></a><i>, a nonprofit newsroom in Chicago that investigates issues of equity and justice in the Cook County court system. </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/subscribe/" target="_blank" ><i>Sign up here to get their weekly newsletter</i></a><i>.</i></p><p>The family of a man with mental illness who died at the Cook County Jail after being beaten by correctional officers has agreed to dismiss a wrongful death lawsuit against the county in exchange for $7.25 million.</p><p>The Cook County Board of Commissioners Finance Committee is set to vote Wednesday on the deal, which if approved by the full board would be the county’s largest single payout for a jail-related lawsuit since at least 2007, according to an Injustice Watch analysis of settlement data.</p><p>The lawsuit revolves around <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/06/28/cook-county-jail-detainee-death-cory-ulmer-beating-handcuffed-sheriff-tom-dart" >the death of 41-year-old Cory Ulmer</a> in June 2024. Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart’s office, which runs the jail, told Ulmer’s family only that he died following a medical emergency, but <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/jail-deaths/2024/cook-county-jail-cory-ulmer-death/" target="_blank" >an internal report</a> leaked to Injustice Watch just days after his demise showed officers repeatedly struck him in the jail’s emergency room after Ulmer became “combative.”</p><p>Records obtained since then show the sheriff’s internal investigators found several officers committed misconduct against Ulmer, with two officers now facing termination. One of those officers had been recommended for firing a decade ago but was allowed to remain on the job, records show.</p><p>Officers began striking Ulmer after he tried running out of a small, bedless holding cell in the jail’s basement known as a “bullpen,” where he had been kept for at least 24 hours awaiting transfer to a psychiatric unit, records show. Officers then dragged Ulmer into the emergency room and witnesses told investigators the officers proceeded to kick, punch, and knee him as he lay facedown, shackled and facing away from security cameras, records show. Ulmer was then injected with sedatives and became unresponsive and was declared dead upon arrival soon after at Mount Sinai Hospital, records show. The Cook County medical examiner ruled his death a homicide.</p><p>Ulmer was taken to jail just a day before he died for violating his court-ordered curfew following 2023 assault and armed robbery charges. The arresting officers with the sheriff’s electronic monitoring unit noted Ulmer was unwell; he was walking on the road shirtless after midnight, and one of the officers speculated Ulmer was “off his meds,” records show. The officers considered taking Ulmer home or to a hospital but took him to the jail instead, records show.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> he died in June 2024. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>llinois State Police</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ulmer’s stepfather, Robert Robinson, <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/jail-deaths/2025/family-sues-cook-county-sheriff-tom-dart-over-brutal-jail-death/" target="_blank" >sued the county</a> in federal court last year, alleging the officers used excessive force against Ulmer in violation of his constitutional rights and that the jail’s medical staff failed to provide him with adequate care or antipsychotic medications, “despite obvious signs that his mental state was deteriorating.” In court filings, the county denied those allegations.</p><p>Ulmer died less than two weeks after Injustice Watch published <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/jail-deaths/2024/cook-county-jail-deaths-2023/" target="_blank" >“Dying on Dart’s Watch,”</a> which revealed inadequate medical care and supervision underlying at least half of the 18 deaths at the jail in 2023. That was the most deaths there in any year since 2013, when the jail’s average daily population was twice as high.</p><p>Since Ulmer’s death, at least another 28 detainees have died at the jail, records show.</p><p>In a statement, Robinson’s attorney, Jesse Guth, said there was “no excuse for the brutality that Cory suffered” and called on lawmakers to open the jail to independent monitoring, to review conditions at the facility for detainees.</p><p>“History will continue to repeat itself until changes are implemented,” Guth said.</p><p>Dart handily won another four-year term in this month’s general election. Citing pending litigation, he declined to be interviewed, as did Dr. Priscilla Ware, medical director of the jail’s healthcare provider, Cermak Health Services. Ware was not a defendant in the lawsuit.</p><h3>Firings, suspensions held up in arbitration</h3><p>The sheriff’s Office of Professional Review closed its internal investigation into Ulmer’s death in December 2025, a year and a half after he died, records show. Investigators probed the actions of 18 correctional officers and said two should be fired and six should be suspended.</p><p>Of the 11 medical staffers named in the lawsuit, one has since left the jail, records show. The others — including doctors, nurses and mental health specialists — continued to work there as of late October. In response to emailed questions, a spokesperson for Cermak Health Services, a division of Cook County Health, did not say whether any of the medical staff had been disciplined.</p><p>Investigators recommended that Sgt. Enrique Reyes and correctional officer Jason Jackson be terminated from their jobs at the jail, records show. Injustice Watch could not reach Reyes and Jackson directly. Their attorneys did not respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Both used unnecessary force against Ulmer, investigators found; a medical staff member who witnessed the beating told investigators that Jackson hit Ulmer the most, and even kicked him in the head multiple times. Investigators also found that Reyes told medical staff to “leave the area” and turned off his body-worn camera during the incident. Reyes told investigators he turned his camera off because Ulmer was about to receive medical attention, but investigators found that to be untrue, records show.</p><p>Jackson’s fate now lies with the sheriff’s Merit Board, a seven-member body appointed by Dart and approved by a majority of county commissioners with final say over firings of correctional officers. Reyes’ firing is before an arbitrator, as is required by the correctional sergeant’s union contract, according to Dart’s spokesperson. In the meantime, both have been stripped of their police powers and were assigned to work at a warehouse, the spokesperson said.</p><p>Reyes and Jackson had each been investigated for misconduct several times prior to Ulmer’s death, according to data provided by Dart’s office through a public records request.</p><p>Investigators recommended that Jackson be fired a year after he was hired in 2016 for allowing detainees to enter a visiting area without permission, and failing to stop those detainees from masturbating in view of visitors. However, his case was instead handled by an arbitrator, who ruled that Dart’s office should reinstate Jackson six months later, according to the sheriff’s spokesperson.</p><p>“Given the fact that Jackson was suspended without pay for approximately 140 workdays … the Sheriff’s Office considered his unpaid suspension to be appropriate disciplinary action and did not initiate further proceedings,” the spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>The sheriff’s internal investigators would go on to sustain misconduct allegations against Jackson in four more disciplinary cases for several policy violations such as using unnecessary force and threatening another person with bodily harm, records show.</p><p>Reyes was investigated on allegations he used excessive force in 2012, 2013, 2014, and 2021, and for allegedly failing to follow policy in 2023. Investigators either exonerated him, closed the investigation without a disposition, or did not sustain the allegations, data show.</p><p>The other six officers with sustained misconduct allegations in Ulmer’s investigation face suspensions ranging from 45 to 120 days for using unnecessary force and being untruthful to investigators, among other policy violations, records show. So far, only one officer has served a suspension, and an arbitrator reduced it from 45 days to five; the rest are still in arbitration, Dart’s spokesperson said. According to investigators, three of those officers failed to report a separate use of force against Ulmer on the morning of the day he died. That incident resulted in Ulmer falling and hitting the back of his head; it was discovered only after the jail’s surveillance team reviewed all of Ulmer’s movements from that day, records show.</p><p>Representatives for the correctional officers’ union, Teamsters Local 700, did not respond to requests for comment. A spokesperson for the correctional sergeants’ union, AFSCME Council 31 Local 3692, said the union does not answer questions about pending grievances.</p><p>Dart’s internal investigators did not look into why jail officials failed to notify the Cook County medical examiner when Ulmer died, records show.</p><p>Under county code, law enforcement officers should “immediately” notify the medical examiner upon a death in custody. The medical examiner then dispatches investigators to the scene to take photos, conduct interviews, and produce a report. The medical examiner was instead notified by a Mount Sinai nurse nearly six hours after Ulmer was pronounced dead, records show. By then, the jail’s emergency room, where officers beat him, had been cleaned.</p><p>In an email, Dart’s spokesperson did not deny jail officials failed to notify the medical examiner but said the sheriff’s office “worked to support every independent investigation conducted by outside agencies in this case.”</p><p>Jail officials enacted a dozen policy changes and directives following Ulmer’s death, including installing cameras to eliminate blind spots in the jail’s hospital, and instructing staff to provide water to detainees in the bullpen, records show.</p><h3></h3><h3>Growing calls for independent oversight</h3><p>The vote to settle the Ulmer lawsuit comes alongside calls for more oversight of the jail and the sheriff’s office.</p><p>Currently, only the Illinois Department of Corrections provides external monitoring of the jail through its jail and detention standards unit, which conducts annual inspections of the facility and issues yearly reports. But advocates and their allies on the Cook County Board of Commissioners say more oversight of the jail is needed to protect people incarcerated there.</p><p>Matthew McLoughlin, a campaign coordinator with the Illinois Network for Pretrial Justice, a coalition working to reduce the number of people incarcerated in jails across the state, said commissioners need more than the once-a-year reports to better understand the conditions in the Cook County Jail. An independent oversight body “would allow for that kind of regular communication,” he told Injustice Watch in an interview.</p><p>In 2025, state inspectors found the jail “violated standards for supervision, security, admissions procedures, reporting, sanitation and more,” the Illinois Answers Project <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisanswers.org/2026/09/15/unsanitary-unsupervised-understaffed-most-illinois-jails-arent-meeting-minimum-state-standards/" target="_blank" >reported</a> in September. Inspectors have cited the jail for violations in six of the past nine years, including every year since 2022, the nonprofit newsroom reported.</p><p>“Obviously, four years in a row of failed inspections, the accountability is not there,” McLoughlin said.</p><p>In an email, Dart’s spokesperson pushed back against the characterization of the sheriff’s office as having “failed” inspections, stressing that inspectors had found the jail to be in compliance with the vast majority of state standards each year.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Meanwhile, jails in cities including New York, Los Angeles, Denver, and Philadelphia are currently under some form of oversight aside from regulatory inspections, research shows.</p><p>In September, Cook County Commissioner Tara Stamps and four co-sponsors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/09/21/cook-county-jail-deaths-commissioners-board" >introduced a resolution</a> calling for an “independent review” of the jail, “focusing on the health, safety and wellness of the detainees and conditions of confinement.” The resolution came nearly two years after <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/jail-deaths/2024/sheriff-tom-dart-county-board-hearing-on-jail-deaths/" target="_blank" >the board held a hearing</a> on jail deaths following Injustice Watch’s reporting. But <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisanswers.org/2026/09/22/cook-county-board-defers-resolution-calling-for-independent-review-of-states-largest-jail/" target="_blank" >Stamps pulled the resolution</a> from a vote in the board’s Health and Hospitals Committee because her colleagues said it could prove to be a legal liability, the Illinois Answers Project reported.</p><p>Injustice Watch obtained an analysis of the resolution done by Cathy McNeil Stein, civil actions bureau chief for the Cook County state’s attorney’s office, and sent to county commissioners a day before they were set to vote. Stein said Stamps’ resolution would be “harmful” to the county’s legal position in pending and future litigation, and would increase its “financial jeopardy.”</p><p>Even if the resolution passed, Stein wrote, the board could not unilaterally order Dart to open the jail to an independent monitor, as state law says Illinois sheriffs have “final policymaking authority over jails in their counties,” citing state law and a circuit court ruling out of DuPage County.</p><p>Stamps told the Illinois Answers Project that she would “retool” and reintroduce the resolution this month, but she had not done so as of publication of this article.</p><p>In an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/11/11/cook-county-jail-independent-review-jamar-boyd-tariq-el-amin-rachel-mikva" target="_blank" >op-ed</a> for the Chicago Sun-Times published last week, a group of interfaith clergy called on commissioners to advance Stamps’ resolution. “The public deserves a clear explanation of how delaying an independent review serves the interests of those in custody and the broader community,” they wrote.</p><p>Stamps did not respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Meanwhile, Dart’s office has also recently come under scrutiny by Tirrell J. Paxton, the county’s independent inspector general.</p><p>In September, records show, Paxton issued six recommendations to the sheriff’s office after a review of more than 100 complaints forwarded to the sheriff’s Office of Professional Review by Paxton and his predecessors found that although the office “generally takes appropriate action,” there were “recurring deficiencies in investigative consistency, documentation, and case management.”</p><p>Dart’s general counsel, Nicholas Scouffas, fired back at Paxton, saying Paxton “did not possess the requisite information, data, understanding, wherewithal, and authority” to make the recommendations, and that the sheriff’s office rejected all of them.</p><p>The county board is now weighing whether to hold a hearing on Paxton’s potential oversight; it has also asked the state’s attorney’s office to provide a legal opinion of the matter.</p><p>Jennifer Vollen-Katz, executive director of prison watchdog group John Howard Association of Illinois, which monitored the jail from 1988 to 2011, told Injustice Watch that more oversight of the jail would ultimately reduce the county’s exposure to lawsuits and “can identify the policies and practices that are leading to these kinds of horrific outcomes that are costing people their lives and costing the taxpayers millions of dollars.”</p><p>“Sometimes just knowing you’re being watched prevents people from behaving badly,” Vollen-Katz said.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-390000" entries.title: Judge tosses man’s murder conviction amid claims of torture led by CPD detective tied to Gitmo abuses
entries.summary: <p>A Cook County judge on Monday threw out the conviction of Anthony Garrett, finding that it’s more likely than not that his written confession in 7-year-old Dantrell Davis’ murder was tortured out of him.</p><p>Circuit Judge Adrienne E. Davis did not mention Richard Zuley, 80, the retired detective accused of orchestrating Garrett’s alleged beating in custody after the boy’s 1992 fatal shooting in a North Side public housing complex.</p><p>“The court vacates the petitioner’s conviction and sentence and suppresses his handwritten statement,” Davis said from her bench at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse, ordering a retrial and a transfer from Illinois custody to Cook County Jail.</p><p>Garrett, 68, was brought into the courtroom in blue prison garb. More than a dozen of his relatives and friends smiled and murmured in the gallery as Davis read aloud portions of a ruling she said was 37 pages.</p><p>Davis ordered a Dec. 7 hearing on Cook County State Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke’s possible appeal of Monday’s ruling, and on Garrett’s detention status.</p><p>Garrett’s attorneys and prosecutors battled in a monthslong evidentiary hearing that ended with closing arguments in May.</p><p>His lead attorney, Jennifer Blagg, argued that retired Chicago Police Detective Richard Zuley, 79, coordinated her client’s torture. She tied the case to alleged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/04/13/settlement-finance-committee-richard-zuley-chicago-detective-carl-reed-coerced-confession" target="_blank" ><u>Zuley-led coercion</u></a> in a string of cases from 1987 to 2003. The cases included four murder convictions later thrown out.</p><p>Blagg also likened Garrett’s interrogation to torture when Zuley was a U.S. Naval reservist at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. She recounted testimony last November by Mohamedou Ould Slahi, who appeared via Zoom from Rotterdam, the Dutch city.</p><p>Slahi, a Sept. 11 terror suspect, alleged that Zuley subjected him to months of torture in 2003 at the notorious detention camp at Guantánamo.</p><p>Slahi, 55, wrote a memoir about the experience that formed the basis of a 2021 film drama starring Jodie Foster and Benedict Cumberbatch.</p><p>“The real Dick Zuley, I would submit to the court, is the one Mohamedou Ould Slahi saw,” Blagg argued in May.</p><p>But O’Neill Burke’s office urged Davis to disregard claims against Zuley in other cases.</p><p>Armando G. Sandoval, one of the prosecutors, called them “allegations, not findings,” and said they had “no connection to Garrett.”</p><p>“I’m not saying everything Slahi says is false,” Sandoval said. “But the court should be careful of treating the book … or the movie as objective.”</p><p>Sandoval also cast doubt on claims by Garrett that two large men wearing sports jerseys beat Garrett at Zuley’s behest while he was shackled to an eyebolt, and that the two men focused many of their blows on a part of his leg where physicians had implanted a rod after a gunshot wound.</p><p>The prosecutor pointed to testimony that Garrett, after his interrogation, was not limping and did not seem to be injured.</p><p>Sandoval pointed to Garrett’s initial claim that the beating took place with a rubber hose. The story changed years later, Sandoval said, when Garrett claimed it was carried out with the hose and a phone book.</p><p>“His account shifts,” Sandoval said. “That’s important.”</p><p>Dantrell was killed on Oct. 13, 1992, as he walked to school with his mother in Cabrini-Green, a former North Side public housing complex. Police said a sniper shot him from an upper floor of a building.</p><p>Garrett, convicted by a jury in 1994, was sentenced to 100 years in prison. Held now at downstate Centralia Correctional Center, he is not scheduled for release until 2039, according to the Illinois Department of Corrections.</p><p>In 2023, an Illinois Torture and Relief Commission finding detailed an “overwhelming” history of “lengthy and consistent” complaints alleging psychological and physical torture involving Zuley, who was hired by the police department in 1970 and worked more than three decades for the department.</p><p>Slahi, who knew Zuley as “Capt. Collins,” testified the detective led<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/11/25/mohamedou-ould-slahi-guantanamo-chicago-police-richard-zuley-anthony-garrett-torture-dantrell-davis" target="_blank" ><u> “enhanced interrogation techniques,”</u></a> including isolation, temperature extremes, beatings, sexual humiliation, sleep deprivation, waterboarding, barking dogs, a mock execution at sea and round-the-clock mistreatment with strobe lights and a looped recording of the U.S. national anthem.</p><p>After 70 days of torture, Slahi testified, and the detective convinced him that U.S. authorities were allowing his mother to be kidnapped and raped. Slahi admitted he never saw Zuley lay a hand on him but added that he wouldn’t know because he was usually blindfolded.</p><p>Slahi testified he eventually confessed to anything his interrogators fed him, starting with plans to attack Toronto’s CN Tower. He said he also falsely confirmed that many individuals had Al Qaeda links.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/04/08/ex-gitmo-detainee-could-air-allegations-of-torture-by-former-chicago-detective" target="_blank" ><u>Slahi was held at Guantánamo</u></a> for 14 years without charges before he was released to his native Mauritania in 2016. His memoirs about those years were published as a book that led to the film, “The Mauritanian,” directed by Kevin Macdonald.</p><p>At the November 2025 hearing, a prosecutor pressed Slahi about visits to Afghanistan in the early 1990s. Slahi answered he was working for U.S. allies there and cut Al Qaeda ties years before the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.</p><p>In Garrett’s case, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/02/19/ex-chicago-det-richard-zuley-denies-torturing-out-confession-to-7-year-old-dantrell-daviss-murder" target="_blank" ><u>Zuley testified</u></a> in February and April. The former detective said he didn’t know of anyone handcuffing Garrett to the eyebolt or subjecting him to any physical or mental abuse.</p><p>Zuley testified he left other detectives in charge of Garrett overnight. The next morning, according to the former detective, Garrett confessed to shooting at members of a rival gang near Dantrell. Garrett later signed a handwritten confession.</p><p>Threats and physical abuse, Zuley testified, were less reliable than “rapport building” for extracting information from suspects.</p><p>Judges have vacated at least four murder convictions involving Zuley. The exonerees are Lathierial Boyd, Lee Harris, Carl Reed and David Wright.</p><p>President Donald Trump’s administration blocked Garrett’s attorneys from questioning Zuley about his work at Guantánamo.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/02/19/ex-chicago-det-richard-zuley-denies-torturing-out-confession-to-7-year-old-dantrell-daviss-murder" >Ex-CPD detective denies torturing confession to Dantrell Davis murder</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/04/08/ex-gitmo-detainee-could-air-allegations-of-torture-by-former-chicago-detective" >Ex-Gitmo detainee could air allegations of torture by former Chicago detective</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2025/11/25/mohamedou-ould-slahi-guantanamo-chicago-police-richard-zuley-anthony-garrett-torture-dantrell-davis" >Ex-Guantánamo detainee testifies a former Chicago detective tortured him for months</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: 'Broadview 6' prosecutors say they won't take the Fifth as potentially explosive hearing looms
entries.summary: <p>Three federal prosecutors who handled the disastrous <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six”</a> case will not invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination when the time comes to testify, their lawyers assured a judge Monday.</p><p>However, it’s unclear how much they’ll be able to say once they’re under oath. That’s the upshot of a 20-minute<b> </b>status hearing<b> </b>that drew Associate Attorney General <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/06/broadview-6-hearing-set-to-rock-chicago-federal-courthouse-but-doj-official-could-intervene" target="_blank" >Stanley<b> </b>Woodward</a>, the Justice Department’s third-highest ranking official, to a Chicago courtroom.</p><p>It’s also unclear what U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros<b> </b>will do.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/06/broadview-6-hearing-set-to-rock-chicago-federal-courthouse-but-doj-official-could-intervene" >Broadview 6 hearing set to rock Chicago federal courthouse, but DOJ official could intervene</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It’s remarkable that federal prosecutors in Chicago even had to consider taking the Fifth. But U.S. District Judge April Perry has<b> </b>ordered<b> </b>them<b> </b>to testify Dec. 2<b> </b>in a hearing with little precedent<b> </b>that could lead to sanctions, or even a finding of criminal contempt.</p><p>Perry used Monday’s status hearing to prepare for the potential testimony.</p><p>In another sign of how the tables have turned, the judge spent much of Monday’s hearing speaking with a new group of lawyers — representing the prosecutors<b> </b>who nearly took the “Broadview Six” case to trial.</p><p>Meanwhile, some of the former defendants watched as spectators from the courtroom gallery.</p><p>The case began as a conspiracy<b> </b>prosecution<b> </b>against<b> </b>six Operation Midway Blitz protesters. It <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >collapsed</a> in spectacular fashion in May amid allegations of prosecutor misconduct. Now, Perry<b> </b>has<b> </b>ordered<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>to<b> </b>testify along with Assistant U.S. Attorneys William<b> </b>Hogan, Matthew<b> </b>Skiba<b> </b>and<b> </b>Andres<b> </b>Almendarez.</p><p>The judge has said her “sole focus, at this point, is on lack of candor, concealment of material facts, or other misconduct that occurred before me.” She’s specifically <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/09/feds-appear-to-hide-name-of-government-lawyer-in-new-broadview-six-court-filing" target="_blank" >raised questions</a> about claims prosecutors made<b> </b>to her while the case played out.</p><p>But in a motion<b> </b>filed<b> </b>late<b> </b>Sunday, Woodward<b> </b>said<b> </b>the four prosecutors<b> </b>have been “instructed”<b> </b>to assert legal privileges, which could prevent them from testifying.</p><p>He argued that “there is plainly no need for anyone but the U.S. attorney to provide information,”<b> </b>and<b> </b>he<b> </b>suggested Perry<b> </b>leave the matter to the executive branch — meaning President Donald Trump and Attorney General Todd<b> </b>Blanche.</p><p>Woodward<b> </b>also floated the possibility<b> </b>that he’ll seek relief from the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/10/broadview-six-boutros-perry-stanley-woodward" >Feds question ‘Broadview 6' judge’s authority as clash over top prosecutor’s testimony inches closer</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>As a result, Monday’s courtroom conversation revolved mostly around the Justice Department’s attempt to assert legal privileges. During the hearing, attorneys for Hogan, Skiba<b> </b>and<b> </b>Almendarez<b> </b>told Perry their clients<b> </b>don’t plan to invoke their Fifth Amendment right.</p><p>Hogan<b> </b>attorney<b> </b>Shelly<b> </b>Kulwin<b> </b>said his client “doesn’t intend to assert any privileges.”</p><p>Perry assured the lawyers she won’t ask questions “that would call for a privileged answer.” Still, she acknowledged the prosecutors might want to offer explanations that cross that boundary.</p><p>So she gave them until Friday<b> </b>to submit a written version of any such testimony for her review. She said she’d give the feds until Nov. 25<b> </b>to explain why privilege should prevent the testimony from going forward.</p><p>Woodward told the judge he was concerned about privileged information<b> </b>being handed over to her ahead of the hearing. He said the Justice Department “may have an issue”<b> </b>with what he described as the judge “wearing dual hats.”</p><p>But Perry said it’s not unusual for a judge<b> </b>to ignore inadmissible evidence<b> </b>that’s come before her.</p><p>And it’s not clear who would decide whether the testimony is privileged, if not Perry.</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks defensemen already learning from new coach Mark Eaton: 'He knows his stuff'
entries.summary: <p>Kevin Korchinski skated off the ice after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> practice Monday having already learned something from Mark Eaton.</p><p>That's a good early sign that the Hawks' decision to move Eaton, one of their assistant general managers, into the coaching staff — to work hands-on with their plethora of young defensemen — could provide fruitful.</p><p>Korchinski said Eaton, who played 650 NHL games (mostly for the Penguins and Predators) from 1999 to 2013 before joining the Hawks' front office, talked to him about being more deceptive with his defensive stick usage.</p><p>"On rush stuff and closing one-on-one, [you can] almost use your stick as a surprise," Korchinski said. </p><p>"You don't want [the opposing player] to know that, for me, I have a long stick. So kind of hide it, hide it, and then when you know you can try to get the puck, that's when you attack. You can surprise a lot of guys that aren't expecting that pressure."</p><p>Since Eaton has long <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/12/10/blackhawks-prospects-anton-frondell-sweden-djurgarden-nhl-ice-time" >overseen</a> the Hawks' prospect development pipeline, he already has preexisting relationships to build upon with every defenseman on the roster except veteran Ian Cole.</p><p>Korchinski recalled having Zoom calls with Eaton back in 2022-23, his final junior-hockey season in Seattle. Then in 2024-25, Korchinski played for Eaton in the AHL, during the latter's stint as Rockford's interim coach — a stint during which Korchinski thought he played "really good hockey."</p><p>"He's really good at knowing each guy individually and knowing what makes you successful and having that happy balance where you play to your strengths but you also work on your weaknesses," Korchinski said. "He's awesome. He knows his stuff. He's very knowledgeable [about] little things that go a long way."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a same thing about Eaton understanding players' strengths.</p><p>"A lot of people just look at someone's weaknesses and say, 'All right, how can we get these better?'" Rinzel said. "But he's really good at knowing what makes players good and using that to [improve] your game."</p><p>And Wyatt Kaiser, who reviewed film with Eaton throughout his three years at Minnesota-Duluth and also briefly played for him in Rockford, mentioned the same thing about Eaton's focus on the "little details" — such as whether to use one or two hands on stick-lifts or when to glance over your shoulder to scan the ice.</p><p>Hawks head coach Jeff Blashill said he first discussed this past summer the idea of adding another defensive-minded coach to support assistant coach Anders Sorensen, who works primarily with the defensemen. The Hawks' two most involved skills coaches, Brian Keane and Chris Kunitz, are both former forwards.</p><p>That idea eventually came to fruition during the Hawks' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/11/blackhawks-kyle-davidson-trades-mark-eaton-jeff-blashill" >soul-searching meetings</a> last week. General manager Kyle Davidson said Eaton's new role will resemble that of an NFL position coach, and Blashill seconded that.</p><p>"When I watch a football practice, man, there's one-on-one coaching," Blashill said. "You don’t need this on certain teams with a whole bunch of veterans, but we have so many young 'D.' We have to maximize this group and try to expedite their growth process."</p><p>Eaton officially started Monday and began getting acquainted with the staff and their messaging, Blashill said. They "work really hard" to communicate and keep that messaging aligned so players don't get confused by contradictory advice from different coaches.</p><p>Nevertheless, it could benefit the defensemen to hear even the same message from a new voice with a fresh perspective, considering things haven't clicked as smoothly as expected so far.</p><p>"We have a coaching staff that's really trying to create a...road map for us," Kaiser said. "To have another guy that comes in, looks at it and tries to communicate it in the way that he thinks we see it, I think it's good."</p>

entries.title: Clientes de Family Dollar en Illinois recibirán pagos de compensación por discrepancias en los precios
entries.summary: <p>Los clientes de Illinois pronto recibirán pagos después de que Family Dollar aceptara un acuerdo de $63 millones por acusaciones de discrepancias de precios en sus tiendas, anunciaron las autoridades el viernes.</p><p>Illinois, la Comisión Federal de Comercio y otros 16 estados demandaron a la empresa, alegando que les cobraba a los clientes más en la caja registradora que los precios anunciados en las estanterías, en las etiquetas y en la publicidad.</p><p>La compañía tendrá que establecer un fondo de compensación de $40 millones para consumidores elegibles y un programa de descuentos de $20 millones para clientes, dijo el fiscal general de Illinois, Kwame Raoul, en un comunicado el viernes. Illinois también recibirá $188,548 como parte del acuerdo.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-290000" name="module-290000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Cobrar de más por productos en un momento en que muchas necesidades básicas se han vuelto menos asequibles perjudica a las familias y comunidades vulnerables”, dijo Raoul en el comunicado.</p><p>“Me complace este acuerdo que responsabiliza a Family Dollar y toma medidas para asegurar que no volverá a cobrar de más a los consumidores en el futuro. Sigo comprometido con proteger a los consumidores de Illinois ante prácticas comerciales injustas”, dijo Raoul en el comunicado.</p><p>La demanda alegaba que miles de tiendas de Family Dollar cobraban de más a los clientes y que la empresa no resolvió el problema pese a repetidas inspecciones fallidas y a quejas de los clientes.</p><p>Family Dollar deberá publicar avisos sobre el fondo de compensación en todas las tiendas y en su plataforma digital, dijo la oficina de Raoul.</p><p>La cadena también tendrá que establecer un programa de verificación de precios que supervise y verifique los precios de forma regular, capacite a los empleados para identificar discrepancias y corrija errores para garantizar que a los clientes se les cobre el precio anunciado o mostrado.</p><p>El programa de verificación de precios será evaluado y certificado de manera independiente cada año.</p><p>Family Dollar no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentario.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: United Airlines says technology issue resolved after widespread system outage delayed outgoing flights
entries.summary: <p>CHICAGO — United Airlines said Monday that it had resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/nationwide-ground-stop-trump-air-travel-faa-6f58e64d9ced2543aaaf7317ec389d06" target="_blank" >nationwide ground stop.</a></p><p>Chicago-based United said in a statement that while some flights were delayed because of the issue Monday afternoon, flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not impacted. It also said, “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”</p><p>United apologized to customers for the inconvenience on social media.</p><p>A recording posted on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.</p><p>The flight tracking website FlightAware showed United with 418 delayed flights late Monday afternoon.</p><p>The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.</p><p>Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.</p><p>United Airlines' app had a message on its home screen stating "We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights. There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights." But it was gone a few minutes later.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p>

entries.title: AI data centers block pollution, climate efforts in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>Demand for electricity to power data centers is hindering the state’s plans to reduce pollution and fight climate change.</p><p>Under <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/9/17/22678787/clean-energy-law-illinois" >an ambitious law</a> signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, the state set out to retire all fossil-fuel power plants between now and 2050.</p><p>But big new data centers are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/12/16/illinois-pritzker-energy-needs-nuclear-gas-power-plants-climate-change-renewable" >requiring so much electricity</a> that it’s become difficult for the state to shut down all coal, gas and oil sources used to meet demand, a pair of state reports released Monday found.</p><p>The reports confirmed fears that environmental and climate advocates have had for more than a year. Cleaner sources of power, including wind and solar farms, are not being built quickly enough to keep up with the new demands from the data centers being used to power artificial intelligence.</p><p>That’s bad news for the planet because oil, gas and coal create carbon dioxide, the major contributor to global warming. The same pollution causing climate change is also bad for our health, causing respiratory problems and exacerbating a number of other threats.</p><p>“Fossil fuel power plants emit thousands of tons of lung-damaging chemicals,” said Brian Urbaszewski, director of environmental health at Respiratory Health Association in Chicago. “These are chemicals that have an immediate and harmful effect on people.”</p><p>In central and southern Illinois, seven coal plants still operate. The goal has been to shut four of them down by 2030 and that goal remains, according to one of the two reports. Three publicly owned coal-fired plants have longer timelines before they are closed.</p><p>Eleven so-called peaker plants, which burn oil or natural gas as power backups, were expected to close in 2030 or 2031. But power demands from data centers mean those plants should continue to operate until 2033 to help prevent blackouts, the report recommends. Those peaker plants are limited-use, oil-fueled or gas-power sources shut down for most days in any given year, but are designed to guard against blackouts and can be fired up when energy use is peaking, like on the hottest day of the year, when many air conditioners are running.</p><p>In Chicago, peakers are still active at the long-closed Fisk coal-fired power plant in Pilsen. There are also peakers in Waukegan, where a former coal plant that has operated for more than 90 years will keep operating until 2033 under the state recommendation.</p><p>“That’s disappointing,” said Mayra Mendez, executive director of Clean Power Lake County. She said the Waukegan peakers produce strong smells that cause a burning sensation in the nose. “Our community is tired of dirty energy.”</p><p>Some advocates feared the state would recommend building new natural gas plants but that is not being advised, state officials said.</p><p>The state will continue to rely on nuclear power and upgrades to plants in hopes of producing more energy which is free of carbon dioxide, according to the reports.</p><h3>Enough power for now</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/energy/2026/10/21/illinois-electric-grid-is-under-a-lot-of-stress-what-does-that-mean-for-consumers" >Illinois is not running out of power yet</a> but the forecast for data centers is so large, and the operations potentially being built so quickly, the situation could create an emergency to provide more electricity.</p><p>Each new hyperscale data center can require enough electricity to power a mid-sized city.</p><p>State lawmakers in Springfield are expected to debate the impact of data centers and power demand, possibly next month.</p><p>Hearings on the state findings are expected later. The reports are the <a class="Link" href="https://ipa.illinois.gov/electricity-procurement/ra-planning/ra-mitigation-plan.html" target="_blank" >Resource Adequacy Mitigation Plan</a> released by the Illinois Power Agency and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency and the <a class="Link" href="https://icc.illinois.gov/informal-processes/Integrated-Resource-Plan" target="_blank" >Integrated Resource Plan</a>, released by the Illinois Commerce Commission.<br></p>
entries.author: Brett Chase

entries.title: Invite this delicata, radicchio and black rice salad to your autumn table
entries.summary: <p>Salads have a place at the table in the fall and winter. When cooler weather invites layering hefty, nourishing ingredients into our meals, this principle also applies to salads. This vibrant salad is layered with nutty black rice, crisp radicchio leaves and roasted delicata squash rings. Bound together in a rich balsamic vinaigrette, each ingredient brings flavor, texture and nutrients to the dish.</p><p>Black rice is also known as forbidden rice or purple rice. It has a mild, earthy flavor and adds striking color to the bowl. Delicata is an oblong squash with green and yellow striated skin, which is edible and nutrient-rich, so there is no need to peel it. When cut into rings, the squash cooks quickly, while the roasting amplifies its sweet and nutty flavor. Choose smaller, narrower squash, so the rings are not too large in the salad.</p><p>This salad is ideal for entertaining, since the components should be prepped ahead of serving and cooled to room temperature. The final assembly takes minutes, which is a cook's gift during the busy holiday season.</p><h3>Delicata, Radicchio and Black Rice Salad</h3><p>Active time: 30 minutes<br>Total time: 30 minutes, plus rice cooking and cooling time<br>Yield: 4 servings</p><p>Ingredients</p><p>Dressing<br>1/3 cup extra-virgin olive oil<br>3 tablespoons balsamic vinegar<br>1 small garlic clove, grated<br>1 teaspoon Dijon mustard<br>1/2 teaspoon kosher salt<br>1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>1 cup black rice, rinsed well<br>Kosher salt<br>1 long, narrow delicata squash, about 1 pound, scrubbed clean<br>1 to 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil<br>1 teaspoon ground cumin<br>1/2 teaspoon ground coriander<br>1/2 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>Pinch of cayenne pepper (optional)<br>1 large head radicchio, cored, leaves torn into shards<br>2 scallions, thinly sliced<br>1/4 cup coarsely chopped Italian parsley leaves<br>2 tablespoons pumpkins seeds and/or pomegranate arils</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Whisk the dressing ingredients in a small bowl.</p><p>Cook the rice until tender, according to package instructions. Season to taste with salt and set aside to cool to lukewarm or room temperature.</p><p>Heat the oven to 425 degrees.</p><p>Cut the squash crosswise in 1/3-inch-thick slices and scoop out the seeds. Place the rings in a large bowl. Add the oil, 1 teaspoon salt, the cumin, coriander, black pepper and cayenne (if using). Toss to coat.</p><p>Arrange the squash rings in one layer on a rimmed baking sheet lined with parchment. Transfer to the oven and roast until golden brown in spots and tender, about 20 to 25 minutes, flipping once.</p><p>Remove from the oven and lightly brush with the dressing. Cool to room temperature.</p><p>Spread the radicchio in a wide, shallow serving bowl. Stir the scallions into the rice and then spoon the rice over and around the radicchio. Arrange the delicata rings around the salad, tucking some of the rings under the radicchio leaves. Sprinkle the parsley and pumpkins seeds and/or pomegranate arils over the salad. Drizzle the dressing to your taste.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i><br></p>
entries.author: Lynda Balslev

entries.title: Step out of the cranberry comfort zone with a reimagined sauce
entries.summary: <p>Tradition has it that a Thanksgiving turkey dinner is not complete without cranberry sauce. Tradition also has it that every November, I find myself scratching my head, trying to reimagine cranberry sauce.</p><p>I have nothing against cranberries, mind you, nor cranberry sauce. I couldn't imagine the holiday table without a heaping bowl of glistening ruby berries simmered into a sweet-tart compote. Yet each year, I make a cranberry sauce and present it at the table. And each year, I wrap up the sauce after our meal, with a good amount untouched, and store it in the refrigerator for goodness-knows-what future purpose. I am not sure if this is a problem unique to my family, or if it's a hushed issue shared by others, too embarrassed to voice their cranberry dysfunction in public. Let me know if you have any insight. Nevertheless, each year, I persevere and make (and write about) some kind of a cranberry sauce — but I always make it with a new twist.</p><p>A straightforward cranberry sauce consists of cranberries and sugar, which I find one-dimensional. Why not step out of the comfort zone and make a jazzy sauce that can be creatively repurposed? I jack up my sauce, transforming it into what could also be called a chutney. It's a condiment that has legs: a tasty, vibrant sauce that will carry you through the entertaining season.</p><p>Chutneys are a raucous sludge of fresh and dried fruit simmered in a sweet, sharp bath of citrus, maybe vinegar and perhaps a splash of spirits; infused with whole spices, savory aromatics and a kick of peppery heat. A sweet, puckery chutney will provide extra bling to your Thanksgiving while seamlessly multitasking beyond the turkey dinner — because, yes, there may be leftovers.</p><p>This recipe is my newest variation of cranberry sauce, with the emphasis on orange. Spread it on a sandwich, serve it on a charcuterie board, dab it on cocktail crostini or spoon a dollop alongside a beef roast or pork loin. Who knows? You might be very pleased this year when you have a lot of cranberry sauce left over after Thanksgiving.</p><h3>Cranberry Orange Chutney</h3><p><b>Active time:</b> 25 minutes<br><b>Total time:</b> 25 minutes, plus overnight chilling<br><b>Yield:</b> About 2 cups</p><p><b>Ingredients</b><br>12 ounces cranberries (fresh or frozen)<br>1/2 cup golden raisins<br>1/2 cup fresh orange juice<br>1/2 cup packed light brown sugar<br>2 tablespoons orange-flavored liqueur, such as Cointreau<br>1 to 2 tablespoons balsamic vinegar<br>1 (2-inch) sprig fresh rosemary<br>1 (2-inch) cinnamon stick3 coins sliced fresh ginger<br>Zest of one orange<br>1/4 teaspoon cloves<br>1/4 teaspoon kosher salt<br>1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Combine all the ingredients in a medium saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring frequently to dissolve the sugar. Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, uncovered, until the cranberries burst and the chutney thickens, about 20 minutes, stirring occasionally.</p><p>Remove from the heat and cool completely. Discard the ginger, rosemary sprig and cinnamon stick. Transfer the chutney to a glass container and refrigerate for at least one day to allow the flavors to develop. Store in the refrigerator for up to one week or freeze for up to one month. Serve at room temperature.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i></p>
